analysis.title: The Stock Market Is The Economy Now: UBS Finds Equity Wealth Effect Running At Twice Dot-Com Peak
key_insights: UBS chief economist Arend Kapteyn says US equities now drive UBS's macro forecasts rather than only result from them. UBS often starts by asking how equities would react to a shock (oil spike, tariffs, AI disappointment), because that reaction alone can swing consumption.

US household holdings of equities and mutual funds are close to 200% of GDP, up from 108% just before the dot-com bust. Pension entitlements add another 110% of GDP. A 10% market move shifts household wealth by about 20% of GDP.

UBS assumes households spend about 6 cents per extra dollar of housing wealth (literature range 2-9 cents) and about 3 cents per extra dollar of equity wealth (survey range 2-5 cents, a recent American Economic Review study 3.2 cents). The inputs come from the Fed's Distributional Financial Accounts.

Excluding the pandemic, the US wealth effect is the largest since before the financial crisis. Housing wealth rose nearly 70% of GDP over nine years before the financial crisis. Equity and mutual fund holdings have risen by the same amount since Q1 2023 alone.
The equity wealth effect is 0.9pp of GDP over the past four quarters. That is almost 3x its 10-year pre-pandemic average and twice its level on the eve of the dot-com bust.
Caveats: lower-income households spend more of their gains but own far fewer stocks, and the shift into 401(k)s locks more of the wealth away until retirement.

The author's own napkin math (not UBS's), assuming a 3% propensity: a 10% drawdown removes about 20% of GDP in household wealth, or about 0.6% of GDP in potential consumption. A 20% bear market removes about 1.2% of GDP in consumption, close to the entire current wealth effect, and enough to tip a slowing economy into recession.
The author argues that equity wealth is concentrated in a handful of AI names, so an AI disappointment, one of the shocks UBS runs through the equity market first, could produce such a drawdown.

risk_factors: A stock market drawdown would reduce household wealth and consumption, and a 20% bear market could tip a slowing economy into recession (author's estimate).
An AI disappointment, an oil spike or tariffs are the shocks UBS now runs through the equity market first, because the equity reaction alone can swing consumption.
Lower-income households spend more of their gains but own fewer stocks, and 401(k) wealth is locked until retirement, which makes the aggregate propensity estimate uncertain.
vol_and_positioning: Household equity exposure at about 200% of GDP means a market drawdown has roughly twice the wealth and consumption impact it would have had in 2000, per the author.
The author notes much of the equity wealth sits in a handful of AI names, which concentrates the downside risk.

tension_points.bull_case: UBS estimates equity wealth is adding 0.9pp of GDP over four quarters, the largest US wealth effect since before the financial crisis, which supports consumption.
tension_points.bear_case: The author says the same math runs in reverse. A 20% bear market would remove about 1.2% of GDP in consumption, near the entire current wealth effect, and equity wealth is concentrated in a few AI names.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A 20% bear market, which the author says would remove about 1.2% of GDP in consumption and could tip a slowing economy into recession.
